# Open science in the lab

Open science makes research plans, methods, code, data, and publications more transparent and easier to find, check, and reuse. This chapter describes practical steps for applying these practices in UAML projects. You can start at any stage and use the practices that fit the project’s design and requirements.

Open science does not mean making every file public. Share outputs when consent, privacy, ethics approval, intellectual property, contracts, and funder rules allow it. When data cannot be public, explain the restriction and consider sharing non-identifying summaries, materials, code, or metadata instead. ULB describes open science as sharing research outputs while meeting these responsibilities. See the [ULB Open Science overview](https://www.ulb.be/en/research/open-science) and its [Research Data Management policy](https://www.ulb.be/medias/fichier/ulb-rdm-policy_1629187645910-pdf?ID_FICHE=7415&INLINE=FALSE).

## Four practices

| Practice | What we do | When |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Preregistration | Record the research questions, hypotheses, design, and planned analyses in a time-stamped registry. | Before data collection, and before analysis when registering a study that uses existing data. |
| Open data and materials | Share a checked, documented version of data and research materials in a repository when sharing is permitted. | Plan access and consent before collection; deposit after checking the files and permissions. |
| Open source code | Share scripts used to prepare, analyze, or model data, with enough documentation to understand and run them. | As the code develops; publish a stable version with the related output. |
| Open access publications | Make the paper freely available through an open access journal or a permitted repository route. | Check journal, funder, and ULB requirements before submission. |

## 1. Plan and preregister the study

Before collecting data, write down the questions and hypotheses, study design, sample size rationale, data-quality rules, exclusions, and primary analyses. Preregister this plan in a suitable public registry such as [OSF Registries](https://help.osf.io/article/330-create-a-preregistration). A preregistration creates a time-stamped record of the plan; it does not prevent legitimate changes. If the study changes, explain what changed, when, and why, and distinguish planned confirmatory analyses from later exploratory work.

### Lab analysis plan

Before data collection or analysis, complete the lab’s **Plan for the analysis.docx** template and save it in the project’s approved shared location. Add the current template link and storage instructions here once the lab confirms them.

Use this checklist when drafting the plan:

- What is the project title, and has any data already been collected?
- What are the research questions and hypotheses?
- What are the variables, conditions, and study design?
- Which analyses directly address the primary questions? Which analyses are secondary?
- How many participants or observations are planned, and how is that number justified?
- What data-quality checks and exclusion rules will be applied?
- For fMRI studies, is the design event-related or blockwise, and how will regions of interest be defined?
- Are there other decisions that should be recorded before the results are known?

### Preregistering computational models

If a project uses a computational model, preregister the modelling decisions as well as the experimental analyses. Record:

- which parameters are free or fixed, their bounds, and the hypotheses about their values;
- the priors for free parameters when using Bayesian estimation;
- which models will be compared and the criterion for selecting among them;
- parameter-recovery simulations, which test whether the fitting procedure can recover known parameter values;
- model-recovery simulations, which test whether the comparison procedure can identify data generated by each candidate model.

For model recovery, report how often data generated by each model are assigned to each candidate model, for example in a confusion matrix. Use the same relevant assumptions and priors in the recovery simulations as in the planned analysis. The lab’s model-specific template and review process still need confirmation. For background, see Crüwell and Evans @crüwell2021 on preregistration for cognitive models and Wilson and Collins @wilson2019 on computational modelling of behavioural data.

## 2. Share data and research materials

Sharing allows others to inspect analyses and, where possible, reproduce or extend the work. Decide what can be shared before collecting data. Check the consent form, participant information, ethics approval, data-access rights, agreements with collaborators, and funder requirements. If participants did not agree to sharing, or the lab does not have permission to share the data, do not release the raw data. Ask the relevant ethics committee or the [ULB Data Protection Officer](https://www.ulb.be/en/being-a-researcher-at-ulb/ethics-committees) if the permitted route is unclear. ULB lists the DPO contact as **rgpd\@ulb.be**.

### Check consent and privacy before deposit

Before a public release:

1.  Confirm that the consent and information materials permit the proposed sharing and reuse.
2.  Confirm that ethics approval and any data-sharing agreements cover the deposit.
3.  Prepare a release copy. Do not upload identifiers or direct exports containing participant IDs, IP addresses, precise timestamps, or identifying free-text responses. Review free-text answers because they may identify a participant indirectly.
4.  Document how you prepared the release copy. Keep the original data in the approved restricted location, and do not treat simple removal of names as proof that a dataset is anonymous.
5.  Ask the ethics committee or DPO to assess whether the release is sufficiently anonymized when this is uncertain.

Anonymized data cannot reasonably be linked back to an individual. Pseudonymized or coded data can still be linked to an individual using additional information, such as a key, and must continue to be protected as personal data. Store any linking key separately with restricted access. ULB’s [ethics and data protection guidance](https://www.ulb.be/en/being-a-researcher-at-ulb/ethics-committees) explains how to seek advice.

When participant-level data cannot be shared, consider whether approved summary statistics, synthetic data, study materials, analysis code, or metadata can be shared without creating unacceptable privacy or security risks.

### Choose a repository and describe the dataset

The current lab guideline identifies [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/) as a repository for sharing data. Confirm that it fits the funder, ULB, ethics, and project requirements before depositing. Zenodo supports record descriptions, access settings, and DOIs for published records; its [deposit guide](https://help.zenodo.org/docs/deposit/) describes the upload and visibility options. Use the repository’s access controls or an approved institutional service when files must remain restricted. Do not put sensitive data in a public record merely to obtain a DOI.

Prepare a README and a data dictionary with each dataset. Include:

- what the files contain and how the folders are organized;
- the number of files, their naming scheme, and which version is the release version;
- what each row and column represents, including variable codes and units;
- how missing values are represented and how the data were selected, cleaned, or transformed;
- which materials and scripts are needed to reproduce the published analyses;
- where access is available, any conditions on reuse, and how to cite the dataset.

The paper’s **master file** should list the variables discussed in the paper. A data dictionary or codebook can serve this purpose. Keep a copy of the final deposited dataset and its DOI with the project records.

### Make the dataset FAIR

FAIR means **Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable**. It describes how to make data easier to discover and use; it does not require unrestricted public access to every dataset.

| Principle | Practical steps |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Findable | Add a clear title, description, creators, keywords, and a persistent identifier such as a DOI when the repository provides one. |
| Accessible | State whether files are downloadable, restricted, or available on request. Explain the access process and any conditions. |
| Interoperable | Use open, documented formats such as CSV, TSV, TXT, or Markdown where appropriate. Keep domain-specific standards such as BIDS when they apply. |
| Reusable | Include a README, codebook, methods, version information, provenance, and a clear licence or reuse condition. Explain missing values and variable codes. |

## 3. Share analysis code

If scripts in R, Python, MATLAB, or another language clean, analyze, or model the data, prepare the relevant code for others to inspect. Include comments where they clarify decisions, and add a README that explains the purpose of each script, required inputs, outputs, run order, software and package versions, and any random seeds used. Remove passwords, access tokens, private file paths, and other confidential information before sharing.

Use the lab’s approved version-control workflow and publish a stable code snapshot with the related paper or dataset. The source guideline mentions Git and GitLab training; add the current lab tutorial link once it has been updated. If code depends on restricted data, share the code separately and explain the access requirements rather than including the data in a public repository.

## 4. Publish open access

Before submitting a paper, check the funder agreement, ULB requirements, journal policy, available institutional agreements, and any publication fees. Common routes include:

- **Open access at publication:** publish in a journal that makes the paper freely available, after checking its policies, licence, and costs. The [Directory of Open Access Journals](https://doaj.org/) can help identify open access journals; indexing is a starting point for checking, not a substitute for reviewing a journal’s scope and practices.
- **Repository deposit:** publish in a subscription journal and deposit a version that the journal and funder permit, such as a preprint or accepted manuscript. Check which version may be shared, where it may be deposited, the licence, and any embargo. Do not assume that the publisher’s formatted version can be shared.

The draft guideline says to consult Julia before submission and also says to “choose the non Open Science route,” while its other sections recommend open access and depositing a preprint. These directions conflict. Confirm the current lab contact and publication procedure before treating either instruction as lab policy. Follow the journal, funder, and ULB requirements for the specific paper. The [ERC Open Science guidance](https://erc.europa.eu/manage-your-project/open-science) explains publication and data requirements for ERC-funded projects; use the grant agreement as the authority for a particular ERC project.

## Project checklist

Before data collection:

- [ ] Complete the analysis plan and preregistration where appropriate.
- [ ] Check whether the consent and participant information allow data sharing and reuse.
- [ ] Record storage, access, backup, retention, and sharing plans in the DMP.
- [ ] Define the data-quality checks, exclusions, and analysis choices.
- [ ] For computational models, plan parameter and model recovery checks where appropriate.

Before sharing or publication:

- [ ] Confirm ethics, consent, permissions, and funder requirements.
- [ ] Prepare and review a release copy; inspect IDs, timestamps, and free text.
- [ ] Add a README, codebook, metadata, version details, and reuse conditions.
- [ ] Check that analysis code can be understood and that confidential information has been removed.
- [ ] Verify the permitted manuscript version, repository, licence, fees, and embargo.
- [ ] Record the DOI or other persistent link in the project files.
